RADON

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
...A DEADLY GAS IN YOUR HOUSE

Unique Selling Point:
Existence of carcinogenic in almost all homes

Summary:
Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after cigarette smoking. Radon is a radioactive gas that forms naturally when uranium, thorium, or radium, which are radioactive metals break down in rocks, soil and groundwater. Overseas strict there are strict regulations. Here nothing (see report on Radon by NNR). Case study: Grant Hatch – stage 4 lung cancer. Areas of concern: Paarl, Mpumalanga, Karoo, any place where there has been mining activity. South Africans need to know about the dangers.

Further information:
Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after cigarette smoking. If you smoke and live in a home with high radon levels, you increase your risk of developing lung cancer. Having your home tested is the only effective way to determine whether you and your family are at risk of high radon exposure.
Radon is a radioactive gas that forms naturally when uranium, thorium, or radium, which are radioactive metals break down in rocks, soil and groundwater. People can be exposed to radon primarily from breathing radon in air that comes through cracks and gaps in buildings and homes. Because radon comes naturally from the earth, people are always exposed to it.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Surgeon General’s office estimate radon is responsible for more than 20,000 lung cancer deaths each year in the U.S. When you breathe in radon, radioactive particles from radon gas can get trapped in your lungs. Over time, these radioactive particles increase the risk of lung cancer. It may take years before health problems appear.
People who smoke and are exposed to radon are at a greater risk of developing lung cancer. EPA recommends taking action to reduce radon in homes that have a radon level at or above 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) of air (a “picocurie” is a common unit for measuring the amount of radioactivity).
Your chances of getting lung cancer from radon depend mostly on:
• How much radon is in your home–the location where you spend most of your time (e.g., the main living and sleeping areas)
• The amount of time you spend in your home
• Whether you are a smoker or have ever smoked
• Whether you burn wood, coal, or other substances that add particles to the indoor air
The chances of getting lung cancer are higher if your home has elevated radon levels and you smoke or burn fuels that increase indoor particles.
CDC’s Radon Communication Toolkit is designed for environmental and public health professionals to use to increase awareness and understanding of radon, its health effects, and the importance of testing for radon among the communities they serve. The toolkit contains customizable fact sheets, infographics, newsletter articles, and social media posts.View large image and text description
Protect Yourself and Your Family from Radon
Having your home tested is the only effective way to determine whether you and your family are exposed to high levels of radon. Steps you can take to measure and reduce radon levels include:
• Purchasing a radon test kit
• Find a Radon Test Kit or Measurement and Mitigation Professionalexternal icon
• Testing your home or office
• Testing is inexpensive and easy — it should only take a few minutes of your time. It requires opening a package and placing a small measuring device in a room and leaving it there for the desired period. Short-term testing can take from a few days to 90 days. Long-term testing takes more than 90 days. The longer the test, the more relevant the results are to your home and lifestyle.
• Sending the kit to appropriate sources to determine radon level
• Follow the directions on the test kit packaging to find out where to send the device to get the results.
• Fixing your home if radon levels are high
• Consumer’s Guide to Radon Reduction: How to Fix Your Home pdf icon[413 KB]external icon
More Ways to Take Action
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development pdf icon[1 MB]external icon recommends additional actions you can take to reduce high radon levels in your home and protect yourself from an increased risk of lung cancer.
For more information on testing your home, check with your state radon officeexternal icon or call the National Radon Hotline at 1-800-SOS-RADON.
• Stop smoking and discourage smoking in your home.
o Smoking significantly increases the risk of lung cancer from radon.
• Increase air flow in your house by opening windows and using fans and vents to circulate air.
o Natural ventilation in any type of house is only a temporary strategy to reduce radon.
• Seal cracks in floors and walls with plaster, caulk, or other mate¬rials designed for this purpose.
o Contact your state radon office for a list of qualified contractors in your area and for information on how to fix radon problems yourself. Always test again after fin¬ishing to make sure you’ve fixed your radon problem.
• Ask about radon resistant construction techniques if you are buy¬ing a new home.
o It is almost always cheaper and easier to build these features into new homes than to add them later.

Script:


V/O:
Fifty three year old Capetonian Grant Hatch is the father of four sons. He married the love of his life Heather 26 years ago, but recent years both Grant and Heather were diagnosed with lung cancer. The news from the doctor was big shock It was a big shock. the shock. of his life. Grant was in shock when his doctor gave him the news.

Grant: I don’t know how to tell you this, but you have cancer.

V/O:
For someone in peak fitness, who had completed 13 Comrades marathons, cancer was unthinkable. Especially odd was the fact that his wife got the same diagnosis. Their lifestyles were quite different and to make sense of it all, he undertook research into causes of lung cancer.
Grant: So what I did, I found on the internet a group, founded by a Norwegian guy, so his wife was diagnosed with cancer, she has got same kind of cancer I’ve got.

V/O:
In the group a gas called Radon kept coming up. Grant had never heard of it. He approached a South African researcher with expertise in Radon. Rayno Botha is a nuclear physicist and the CEO of CareTac, a company that provides radioactive testing.

Ryno: Radon is a natural occurring radioactive gas, and I would like to emphasise that it is naturally occurring. It is not produced in a nuclear power plant, it is not produced in isotope production facility. It’s natural. We don’t, we can’t use any of our human senses to detect it. You can’t small it, you can’t taste it.

V/O:
Radon is formed when Uranium decays, and is found in the ground, in rocks, even in water. It is radioactive and emits Alpha radiation. It is considered a Category 1A cancer causing agent.

LINK:
Radon can enter your home in many ways.
Radon seeps from the ground and can also enter a house through air and ground water. If ventilation is poor, it can accumulate to dangerous levels.

V/O:
Both Grant and Botha tested his current home.

Grant: And then we couldn’t find anything here, and I said no, it’s not here, so I went out to our farmhouse and I found it there. 480 becquerels per cubic meter in that house.
V/O:
Radon concentration is measured in becquerels per cubic metre. Acceptable levels according to the World health organization, is around 200. Botha tested the farmhouse near Barrydale, where Grant and his family had lived for 15 years.

Ryno: We were quite shocked, we did measurements and it was about 10 times as high as what you would find in an average condition it was quite high

Voice:
Grant’s wife Heather was diagnosed in March 2018 and died three months later. A statistician friend at Cambridge University worked out that the odds of both Grant and Heather getting lung cancer, at the same time, of natural causes, was one in 7.5 billion. Grant was convinced it was because of the Radon in their farmhouse.

Professor Michael Herbst, is the spokesperson for the Cancer Association of South Africa.
Michael: Radon Gas is the second most important cause of lung cancer, worldwide, following on tobacco usage and that is very scary.

V/O:
It’s scary because Radon is a gas that is inhaled.

Michael:
The radon usually attaches itself to small particles in the air, like dust particles. One inhales it, it is electrically charged charged, so it attaches itself to the most lower part of the lungs, there where the cells are single layer cells in those cells where oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange takes place. And we must remember that it is alpha rays, so they can only penetrate very single layer cells, and that is where they do their damage and they cause DNA damage right down in the lungs, and that is why Radon is such an important cause of lung cancer.

V/O:
The link between Radon and lung cancer is such a well-established medical fact that internationally many countries require property transactions to include a Radon compliance certificate – much like electricity compliance certificates in South Africa. Because South Africa is so rich in minerals, radon is known to occur at dangerous levels throughout this country. The only available comprehensive study on indoor levels of the gas took place in 2002. Remember a reading of 200 Becquerels or less is considered acceptable. Maximum levels recorded were 842 in the Paarl, 595 in Parys, 440 in Randburg, 393 in Nababeep, 273 in Krugersdorp. And we know that In the Hatch’s farmhouse near Barrydale readings peaked near 500.

Ryno:
We can expect one in 15 houses in South Africa to contain high Radon concentrations.

V/O:
A frightening figure, based on international statistics research – and few people are aware of it.

LINK:
BUT In other countries like the US legislation around Radon Gas has been in place for at least 70 years.

Voice:
In South Africa there are no regulations.

This in spite of the fact that the gold mining industry is notorious for contaminating land with radioactive waste. Mariette Liefferink of the Federation for a Sustainable Environment says that the Witwatersrand’s 270 mine dumps are radioactive.

Mariette:
So the 270 tailings storage facilities or mine dumps, within the Witwatersrand, contains 600,000 tons of Uranium.

V/O:
And where there is Uranium, there is Radon. Carte Blanche has reported extensively on this problem. Hundreds of thousands of people in informal settlements live on or near contaminated sites, such as the notorious Tudor and Lancaster Dams and the Tudor Shaft. But despite the massive risk to human life, there’s little action on the ground.

Mariette: In 2009 it was recommended that it should be urgently remediated or rehabilitated. We are now in 2019, 10 years later and here has been no rehabilitation. Not only that, but it is not fenced, no warning signs, no access control.

LINK:
Issues around Radon gas are complex, but the buck has to stop somewhere. But who is ultimately responsible for addressing the problem?

V/O:
The answer is simple: the National Nuclear Regulator. This statutory body has in recent years introduced sterling regulations for the mining industry, but none protecting the public from radiation and Radon. John Pule heads up the Department for Environmental and Radiation Protection at the NNR.We approached him to find out more about Radon gas.

Devi:
And where does it occur? Any hotspots?

John: At this stage, I need to say to you that, in South Africa, we have actually not done a substantial work to determine, to the extent that we will be able to determine ‘hotspots’ if any.

Devi:
My concern is, we should have been working on this a while ago.
John: One of the things that we are working on at this stage, there is what we called the National Radon Action Plan. So, in the National Radon Action Plan, essentially what we will be doing is, putting together a document to identify, that scopes this problem, and then identify all the necessary sub-projects and projects that needs to be undertaken.

Devi:
John, I know it sound like I’m hammering on this question, but I have to pitch it to you again, Radon, not good for human health, Uranium not good for human health, those are facts. I still don’t understand where we as the National Nuclear Regulator, it is taking us so long, we aren’t even at a point where we have any kind of legislation. It takes a long time to make legislation in any country. I am trying to figure out how we can save people’s lives here.

John:
I do not want to suggest, people’s lives, remember, we have to work on, at this stage, we are saying theoretically there could be a problem, We need go and on the ground and quantify.

V/O:
It seems that regulations are very far off – even research is in the planning stages. But, in the absence of regulations, it is possible to take measures to mitigate against high Radon levels in your home.
The US Department of Housing suggests the following measures to limit the risk:
• Test your house regularly
• Make sure every room is well ventilated
• Seal cracks in floors and walls
• Use radon resistant construction techniques

V/O:
John Pule says the NNR has a Public Outreach effort to inform the public about radiation but he could not specify how many people have been reached. While the NNR seems uncertain about the scope of the problem, and has decided to do more research, regulations to protect the public against Radon, have been delayed.

John:
Our hope is that ultimately, after we have done the studies, the answer is pheww! you do not have a problem.

V/O:
For now, Grant Hatch has decided to fight the lung cancer with all he has, and remains convinced that the disease was caused by Radon.

John:
If I had known of the risks of Radon, my wife would still be alive today, and I would have to be a single father looking after 4 boys. That’s the reality of this.

It takes a long time to make legislation in any country. I am trying to figure out how we can save people’s lives here. John: I do not want to suggest, people’s lives, remember, we have to work on, at this stage, we are saying theoretically there could be a problem, We need go and on the ground and quantify. V/O: It seems that regulations are very far off – even research is in the planning stages. But, in the absence of regulations, it is possible to take measures to mitigate against high Radon levels in your home. The US Department of Housing suggests the following measures to limit the risk: • Test your house regularly • Make sure every room is well ventilated • Seal cracks in floors and walls • Use radon resistant construction techniques V/O: John Pule says the NNR has a Public Outreach effort to inform the public about radiation but he could not specify how many people have been reached. While the NNR seems uncertain about the scope of the problem, and has decided to do more research, regulations to protect the public against Radon, have been delayed. John: Our hope is that ultimately, after we have done the studies, the answer is pheww! you do not have a problem. V/O: For now, Grant Hatch has decided to fight the lung cancer with all he has, and remains convinced that the disease was caused by Radon. John: If I had known of the risks of Radon, my wife would still be alive today, and I would have to be a single father looking after 4 boys. That’s the reality of this.

metadata.Further information: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after cigarette smoking. If you smoke and live in a home with high radon levels, you increase your risk of developing lung cancer. Having your home tested is the only effective way to determine whether you and your family are at risk of high radon exposure. Radon is a radioactive gas that forms naturally when uranium, thorium, or radium, which are radioactive metals break down in rocks, soil and groundwater. People can be exposed to radon primarily from breathing radon in air that comes through cracks and gaps in buildings and homes. Because radon comes naturally from the earth, people are always exposed to it. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Surgeon General’s office estimate radon is responsible for more than 20,000 lung cancer deaths each year in the U.S. When you breathe in radon, radioactive particles from radon gas can get trapped in your lungs. Over time, these radioactive particles increase the risk of lung cancer. It may take years before health problems appear. People who smoke and are exposed to radon are at a greater risk of developing lung cancer. EPA recommends taking action to reduce radon in homes that have a radon level at or above 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) of air (a “picocurie” is a common unit for measuring the amount of radioactivity). Your chances of getting lung cancer from radon depend mostly on: • How much radon is in your home–the location where you spend most of your time (e.g., the main living and sleeping areas) • The amount of time you spend in your home • Whether you are a smoker or have ever smoked • Whether you burn wood, coal, or other substances that add particles to the indoor air The chances of getting lung cancer are higher if your home has elevated radon levels and you smoke or burn fuels that increase indoor particles. CDC’s Radon Communication Toolkit is designed for environmental and public health professionals to use to increase awareness and understanding of radon, its health effects, and the importance of testing for radon among the communities they serve. The toolkit contains customizable fact sheets, infographics, newsletter articles, and social media posts.View large image and text description Protect Yourself and Your Family from Radon Having your home tested is the only effective way to determine whether you and your family are exposed to high levels of radon. Steps you can take to measure and reduce radon levels include: • Purchasing a radon test kit • Find a Radon Test Kit or Measurement and Mitigation Professionalexternal icon • Testing your home or office • Testing is inexpensive and easy — it should only take a few minutes of your time. It requires opening a package and placing a small measuring device in a room and leaving it there for the desired period. Short-term testing can take from a few days to 90 days. Long-term testing takes more than 90 days. The longer the test, the more relevant the results are to your home and lifestyle. • Sending the kit to appropriate sources to determine radon level • Follow the directions on the test kit packaging to find out where to send the device to get the results. • Fixing your home if radon levels are high • Consumer’s Guide to Radon Reduction: How to Fix Your Home pdf icon[413 KB]external icon More Ways to Take Action The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development pdf icon[1 MB]external icon recommends additional actions you can take to reduce high radon levels in your home and protect yourself from an increased risk of lung cancer. For more information on testing your home, check with your state radon officeexternal icon or call the National Radon Hotline at 1-800-SOS-RADON. • Stop smoking and discourage smoking in your home. o Smoking significantly increases the risk of lung cancer from radon. • Increase air flow in your house by opening windows and using fans and vents to circulate air. o Natural ventilation in any type of house is only a temporary strategy to reduce radon. • Seal cracks in floors and walls with plaster, caulk, or other mate¬rials designed for this purpose. o Contact your state radon office for a list of qualified contractors in your area and for information on how to fix radon problems yourself. Always test again after fin¬ishing to make sure you’ve fixed your radon problem. • Ask about radon resistant construction techniques if you are buy¬ing a new home. o It is almost always cheaper and easier to build these features into new homes than to add them later.
